stem:
A new orally administered antiepileptic drug is being evaluated in a phase I clinical trial.  Initial studies in animals show the drug undergoes extensive metabolism by hepatic glucuronosyltransferase, creating a drug-glucuronide metabolite that is renally excreted.  The graph below demonstrates how the rate of glucuronidation (ie, amount of drug glucuronidated per unit of time) changes as increasing doses of the drug are given.

Which of the following is the most accurate statement about this drug's metabolism?​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌

options.label: A
options.text: A constant percentage of the drug present is metabolized per unit of time at point 3

options.label: B
options.text: Bioavailability of the drug is highest at point 1

options.label: C
options.text: Biotransformation of the drug ceases at point 2

options.label: D
options.text: Metabolism is transitioning from first-order to zero-order kinetics at point 2

options.label: E
options.text: The rate of drug metabolism is independent of dose at point 1

explanation:
Drug-metabolizing enzymes such as glucuronosyltransferase have a limited capacity, so the kinetics of drug metabolism can change as the dose increases.  The graph shows this pattern: the glucuronidation rate initially rises linearly with dose, then increases more slowly, and finally plateaus.  At lower doses (point 1), the rate of drug glucuronidation is directly proportional to the dose administered; as more drug is given, more drug-glucuronide is produced per unit of time (Choice E).  Because a fixed percentage of the drug is metabolized per unit of time (eg, 10 mg of a 20-mg dose or 20 mg of a 40-mg dose, both 50%), this early portion of the graph represents first-order kinetics.

At higher doses, a substantial fraction of the enzyme's active sites becomes occupied, so further dose increases produce progressively smaller rises in glucuronidation rate.  Point 2 lies on the curved portion of the graph, where metabolism is transitioning from first-order to zero-order kinetics.  Once the enzyme is saturated (point 3), glucuronidation proceeds at its maximal rate (Vmax), and a fixed amount of drug is metabolized per unit of time regardless of dose (eg, 50 mg whether the dose is 300 mg or 600 mg).  This is zero-order kinetics.  Drugs with saturable metabolism (eg, phenytoin, ethanol, high-dose aspirin) can therefore show disproportionately large increases in plasma concentration with small dose increases.

Zero- and first-order kinetics can also be represented graphically by showing the decrease in drug concentration over time after a single dose.  Zero-order kinetics is indicated by a straight line with negative slope (fixed amount eliminated per unit of time), whereas first-order kinetics manifests as an exponential decay curve (fixed percentage eliminated per unit of time).

(Choice A)  At point 3, the curve is flat, indicating that the same amount of drug is metabolized per unit of time regardless of dose.  This fixed amount therefore represents a progressively smaller percentage of each larger dose (eg, 50 mg is 17% of a 300-mg dose but only 8% of a 600-mg dose).  If a constant percentage were metabolized, the glucuronidation rate would continue to rise linearly with dose, as it does at point 1, rather than plateauing.

(Choice B)  Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered drug that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged.  It usually decreases with oral administration due to incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism compared to intravenous administration.  In this study, higher doses of the drug are likely to have greater bioavailability due to saturation of hepatic glucuronidation.  Bioavailability would therefore be lowest, not highest, at point 1.

(Choice C)  At point 2, the glucuronidation rate is still rising with dose, only more slowly as the enzyme approaches saturation.  Even at point 3, drug metabolism continues at a fixed maximal rate rather than stopping.

Educational objective:In first-order kinetics, a fixed percentage of drug is metabolized per unit of time, so the amount metabolized changes based on the serum concentration.  In zero-order kinetics, a fixed amount of drug is metabolized per unit of time, independent of serum levels.  Drugs metabolized by saturable enzymes shift from first-order to zero-order kinetics as the dose increases and the enzymes become saturated.​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌
